title: Solving the pooling problem at scale with extensible solver GALINI
contribution: A Pyomo pooling-network library that keeps the network structure with the model and feeds a Luedtke et al. convex relaxation (cut generator) and a Dey-Gupte MIP restriction (primal heuristic) into the extensible solver GALINI as opt-in plug-ins, giving smaller gaps than Gurobi 9.1 on the largest dense pooling instances and losing on sparse ones (read as arXiv v1).
problem_entry: Solvers see 'flat' problems; detecting pooling structure is a heuristic that may miss user structure (the prior detector found pooling in 6% of MINLPLib), so carry the structure from the modelling layer to solve larger pooling instances (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Store the pooling network inside a Pyomo smart block and let class-specific plug-ins (Luedtke relaxation/cuts, Dey-Gupte MIP restriction) use it through GALINI's runtime entry-point interfaces without changing GALINI (pp. 2, 6-16).
assumptions: Three-layer pooling-like network, not validated, extra edges ignored (pp. 7-8); heuristic needs linear side constraints (pp. 15-16); relaxation built only at the root on 'preliminary results' (p. 16); tau = 1, 60 s, 1% gap for the heuristic (p. 15).
proof_devices: No theorems; validity of inequalities (11)-(14) cited from Luedtke et al. 2020 (pp. 10-11)
Gradient (outer-approximation) cuts for convex quadratic inequalities generated only when violated by epsilon (p. 12)
McCormick envelope of the scaled product r = s p (eqs. (3)-(6), p. 10)
Restriction kept a true restriction: nonlinear side constraints not dropped, failure raised instead (p. 16)
experiments: Laptop i7-6700HQ; GALINI 1.0.1 (CPLEX 12.10, Ipopt 3.13.2) vs Gurobi 9.1 NonConvex=2, 600 s, gaps 1e-6/1e-8; 360 sparse Haverly-based + 50 dense randstd instances; Gurobi in six configurations incl. time-counted and oracle cuts/warm start; performance profiles on time and gap, shifted geometric means, a difficult subset, LB/UB breakdown; GALINI not competitive on sparse, wins the gap 9/10 on the largest dense groups via a 28% better upper bound (pp. 16-23, 28-35).
positioning: Continues Misener-Floudas pooling and the 2016 detector; places itself in the MIP network-detection lineage; reuses Luedtke et al. and Dey-Gupte as components, confirms Dey-Gupte and dates the Luedtke gain to an older Gurobi (pp. 2, 19).
writing: Software-paper register with interface lists, tables and code appendices; abstract claim scoped to the largest instances; negatives stated in results and conclusion (pp. 1, 6, 21, 23, 35-42).
limits_future: GALINI B&B node throughput much slower than Gurobi's (p. 21); heuristic fails with nonlinear side constraints (pp. 15-16); relaxation not updated in the tree (p. 16); future: other network problems such as optimal power flow, combining with detection (pp. 2, 7).

title: Formulating data-driven surrogate models for process optimization
contribution: A short joint perspective with Biegler that frames data-driven surrogates for process optimisation by two conditions (no extrapolation, no overfitting), three levels of surrogacy, surrogate-led vs mathematical-programming-led choice, a survey of MIP/NLP formulations per surrogate class, trust-region-filter verification and software (read in a 6-page conference-format version).
problem_entry: A new wave of data-driven optimisation raises what must hold for a surrogate inside process optimisation and how to verify that the surrogate optimum is the truth-model optimum (p. 1).
key_idea: Organising frame: Conditions 1-2 tied to Lipschitz stability, plant/unit/property levels of surrogacy with equation-level trade-offs, two perspectives, a formulation survey (polynomial, ReLU, trees, GPs), TRF verification (pp. 1-4).
assumptions: TRF guarantees need truth models with smooth input-output properties (p. 4); DFO methods discussed are unconstrained (p. 3); robustness tied to Lipschitz continuity and parameter confidence regions (p. 1).
positioning: Mathematical-programming view justified by the SGD/stationarity gap (Zhang et al. 2022); global DFO ranked below spatial B&B for lacking lower bounds; own tools (OMLT, ENTMOOT) listed alongside reluMIP, ALAMO, ARGONAUT (pp. 2-4).
writing: Bulleted two-perspective framing, numbered conditions, the aphorism 'all models are imperfect, but some are useful', a two-sentence conclusion (pp. 1, 3, 4).
limits_future: Open: DNN/SGD vs large-scale optimisation for process models (p. 2), smoothing ReLU via complementarity (p. 3), TRF with model mismatch and noise (p. 4); limits of the framing itself not discussed.

method_links.note: Trained surrogates written as MIP/NLP formulations and added to Pyomo via OMLT/reluMIP; Condition 1 (constrain against extrapolation) is the stated form of step 4

title: Combining multi-fidelity modelling and asynchronous batch Bayesian Optimization
contribution: A modular asynchronous multi-fidelity batch BO algorithm (multi-task GP, any acquisition function made batch-aware, a separate variance- or information-based fidelity selector, a per-fidelity batch-space budget) with a review and an empirical study on synthetic, 40D and BASF battery-derived benchmarks (read as arXiv v2).
problem_entry: Battery-lab BO breaks two classical assumptions (single source, sequential results); combining multi-fidelity with batching necessarily creates asynchronicity, which becomes the setting (pp. 1-2, 9).
key_idea: Pick the input with any batch-modified acquisition function on the target fidelity, then pick the fidelity with a cheap selector (variance threshold or cost-weighted MF-MES evaluated M times), under a batch-space budget (pp. 10, 12-13).
assumptions: Two or three fixed fidelities, known scalar costs, delays, Gaussian noise; MF-GP-UCB needs known bias bounds, LMC does not; Lipschitz penalizers with estimated L; quasi-normalised outputs for gamma = 0.1 (pp. 4, 6-7, 9-10, 13).
proof_devices: Tightest of M fidelity UCBs (eq. (9), p. 6)
Lipschitz-ball and hard local penalizers (eq. (17), p. 9)
Lipschitz constant estimated from the GP posterior gradient mean, locally (p. 14)
Fantasies re-train only the GP mean since the posterior variance depends only on input locations (p. 8)
experiments: Log-regret vs time-step; Currin2D, BadCurrin2D, Hartmann3D/6D, Park4D, Borehole8D (batch 4), Ackley 40D (batch 20), a battery benchmark from GP samples of anonymised BASF data; ten methods; baselines batch-filled randomly for fairness; TuRBO fails on Park4D/Borehole8D, independent GPs good on the battery problem, BNNs dropped, MF-MES/TuRBO omitted where infeasible; number of repetitions not stated (pp. 5, 14-19, 25-27).
positioning: Builds on Kandasamy et al. 2016a and generalises Takeno et al. 2020 to avoid its cost and single-acquisition lock-in; contrasts with the Li et al. 2021 BNN approach; Table 1 strengths/weaknesses review (pp. 2-3, 11).
writing: Numbered contributions I-III, half tutorial review, everyday analogies, closes with an Occam's-razor argument for the simple robust method (pp. 2, 9, 19).
limits_future: Multiple cost types and multi-objective acquisition left to future work (pp. 6, 12); acquisition choice an open problem (p. 19); fixed thresholds need output scaling (p. 13).

title: Optimizing over trained GNNs via symmetry breaking
contribution: Symmetry-breaking constraints for optimisation over trained GNNs with non-fixed input graphs, proved never to remove all representatives via a constructive indexing algorithm, plus bilinear and big-M MIP formulations for a general GNN class in OMLT, tested on QM7/QM9 molecular design (read as arXiv v2).
problem_entry: The inverse problem over trained GNNs (molecular design) is little studied; permutation invariance, useful for prediction, creates N! symmetric solutions that hamper B&B (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Break symmetry on abstract nodes with (S1) connectivity, (S2) a minimal-feature node 0 and (S3) lexicographically ordered neighbour sets, linearised by powers-of-two coefficients, instead of relying on solver symmetry detection on the full MIP (pp. 3-9).
assumptions: Undirected graphs with node features; GNN layers of form (star) with linear aggregation and constant weights/biases; bounded features for big-M; molecules without aromaticity/radicals, fixed N; composition bounds from the data set (pp. 3, 7-8, 22, 25).
proof_devices: Lexicographic order on multisets by padding to fixed-length sequences (pp. 3-4)
Constructive indexing Algorithm 1 with temporary indexes and neighbour sets (p. 4)
Properties 1-3 and Lemma 1 (temporary order respects final order) (pp. 4-5, 17-18)
Theorem 1 by contradiction at the minimal violating index, two cases (pp. 5-6)
Worked example showing why temporary indexes are needed (pp. 19-21)
experiments: Solution-pool counting of feasible structures (removal 40-41% at N=2 up to >=98% at N=6; Table 1, p. 9); 5 kept GNNs x 10 Gurobi seeds = 50 runs per N and formulation, Gurobi 10.0.1, 10 h; success counts, mean/Q1/Q3 of time to tolerance and time to optimum, presolve sizes; e.g. QM7 N=7 big-M 0/50 vs 49/50 with symmetry breaking; big-M faster in 341/500 runs (pp. 9-10, 25-27).
positioning: Generalises Mc Donald's GraphSAGE big-M formulation; contrasts with solver-side symmetry detection (BLISS, orbital fixing) that sees only the MIP graph; presents (S3) as a non-trivial generalisation of orbitope lexicographic constraints (pp. 2, 6-7).
writing: Paper-structure paragraph, theorems in the body with proofs in the appendix, engineering choices labelled as such, explicit Limitations and Future-work paragraphs, reviewers thanked (pp. 2, 4-6, 8, 10).
limits_future: Constant weights/biases exclude some GNN types; MIP limits GNN size and edge features enlarge it; QM9 N=8 only 29/50 solved; future: edge features, more architectures, other isomorphism-invariant functions, aromaticity, larger molecules (p. 10; Table 7, p. 27).
